entities.name: Konrad I, Duke of Głogów
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Konrad I, Duke of Głogów, a pivotal figure in the post-Mongol fragmentation of Silesia, ruled the nascent Duchy of Głogów from approximately 1249/50 until his death in 1273. Born into the powerful Silesian Piast dynasty as the third son of Henry II the Pious and Anna of Bohemia, Konrad's life was defined by the complex inheritance disputes that followed his father's demise at the Battle of Legnica in 1241. His persistent efforts to secure a distinct territorial domain for himself against his elder brothers, Bolesław II Rogatka and Henry III of Wrocław, profoundly shaped the political map of Lower Silesia, solidifying the trend of ducal partition that characterized the region for centuries.

Konrad's claim to Głogów was not easily won. Initially destined for an ecclesiastical career, he was educated in Paris and served as Provost of Wrocław Cathedral, but abandoned his clerical path following his father's death to pursue a secular inheritance. After years of intense fraternal conflict and strategic alliances, including a temporary pact with his brother Bolesław II against Henry III, Konrad finally secured the Duchy of Głogów through a series of treaties and military maneuvers by 1249/50. His reign saw the consolidation of this new duchy, fostering its internal development and engaging in a delicate balance of power politics with neighboring Piast dukes and the rising influence of the Bohemian crown under Ottokar II Přemysl. He actively supported the colonization of his lands through German settlers, a common practice among Silesian Piasts, contributing to the region's economic and demographic growth.

entities.name: Konrad I, Duke of Głogów
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Konrad I, Duke of Głogów (c. 1229 – 6 August 1273), a pivotal figure among the Silesian Piasts, carved out the autonomous Duchy of Głogów amidst the turbulent political landscape of 13th-century Central Europe. As the fourth son of Henry II the Pious, Duke of Silesia, and Anna of Bohemia, Konrad's life was defined by the relentless fragmentation of the Polish Piast realm, transforming a once unified ducal territory into a mosaic of smaller, often rivalrous, principalities. His reign, lasting from 1249/50 until his death, established Głogów as a distinct political entity, influencing the regional balance of power in Silesia.

Following the catastrophic Mongol invasion and his father's death at the Battle of Legnica in 1241, Konrad engaged in a protracted struggle with his elder brothers, Bolesław II Rogatka and Henry III the White, over their shared inheritance. Initially destined for the Church, Konrad abandoned his ecclesiastical path to claim his secular birthright. Through shrewd diplomacy, alliances, and intermittent military confrontation, he successfully asserted his claim to Głogów, securing its formal independence by 1249/50. His rule saw the continued development of urban centers under German law (Magdeburg Law), the encouragement of German settlement (Ostsiedlung), and the strategic fortification of his nascent duchy, laying administrative and economic foundations for generations.
